As the receipt/inbound/coexistence logs grow, every consumer catch-up page and every retention purge degrades linearly.
issues.failure_scenario: A high-volume tenant accumulates millions of receipt rows. A consumer paging /internal/notifications/receipts (limit 200) causes Postgres to bitmap-scan and sort all receipt rows on each page instead of a keyset seek, so catch-up reconciliation latency grows with total log size and can time out / starve the pool.

issues.title: Welcome-credit expiry is silently dropped — promo grants never lapse
issues.detail: The adapter only sets an expiry via body['expires_at'] = request.metadata.get('expires_at'), but GrantService.issue() builds the GrantRequest with metadata={'once_per': once_per} and never puts 'expires_at' in metadata (grants.py:99). The configured `days` (spec.get('days')) is used only as the gate `if request.days:` and is never converted to an absolute instant anywhere. So whenever a grant has days>0 configured, the wallet credit is sent with expires_at=None (or omitted), meaning wallet-service's sweep-grants job can never reclaim it. The docstring's promise ('expires_at makes it a grant rather than a gift ... computing it here keeps the expiry in one place') is unimplemented.
issues.failure_scenario: A flow grants a 90-day welcome credit (spec has amount+days=90). Customer claims it. The wallet Grant is created with no expires_at, so it never lapses and the nightly sweep never claws back the unspent remainder. Every welcome credit becomes a permanent, unbounded promotional liability — the exact drain the design set out to prevent.

issues.title: Resume of failed compensation loses the reference and silently abandons cleanup
issues.detail: When an undo raises, _compensate records only {'step': step.name, 'error': str(exc)} — it drops step.result (the created resource's reference). ProvisioningService.resume() then calls provisioner.undo(request, entry.get('reference', '')) with an EMPTY reference (provisioning.py:147). HttpProvisioner.undo returns ProvisionResult(status=CREATED, detail='nothing was created') when reference is empty (provisioner/http.py:57-58), whose .ok is True (ports/provisioner.py:55). resume() therefore treats the undo as successful and drops the entry from the still-unfinished list, marking the run clean while the downstream resource (tenant/membership) was never actually deleted.
issues.failure_scenario: Provisioning creates a tenant then a membership; membership create fails; the tenant undo fails because wallet/tenant-service is briefly down, so the tenant lands in 'unfinished' (without its reference). Operator later calls /admin/resume/{subject}. resume passes an empty reference, undo no-ops as 'nothing was created', resume reports resumed=True with empty unfinished — and the orphan tenant survives forever, with the record now claiming rollback is complete.

issues.title: Grant scope default diverges between issue (tenant) and satisfaction check (user)
issues.detail: claim_grant issues with scope=spec.get('scope','tenant') (api/v1/onboarding.py:112) and GrantService.mark_granted stores the local fact under a tenant-scoped key when scope=='tenant' (local_facts.py:52). But LocalFacts.check resolves scope with `tenant if req.get('scope')=='tenant' else f'{tenant}:{subject}'` (local_facts.py:38), defaulting to SUBJECT scope. For a grant requirement that declares no explicit scope, the grant fact is WRITTEN at key 'req::tenant' but READ at key 'req::tenant:subject' — the two never meet.
issues.failure_scenario: A flow has a requirement with grants set but no scope field. Customer claims the grant: the wallet credit is issued and the ledger records it, mark_granted writes the tenant-scoped key. On the next /next call the requirement is re-evaluated, LocalFacts.check reads the subject-scoped key, finds nothing, and reports it UNSATISFIED. The flow permanently shows the gift as outstanding; re-claiming hits the ledger dedupe (ALREADY) but still never flips the requirement satisfied.

issues.title: DSAR erasure never matches onboarding_grants rows — subject data silently retained
issues.detail: erase() filters onboarding_grants with where={'tenant':tenant,'subject':subject}, but LocalFacts.mark_granted writes rows containing only {'id','reference','at'} — no 'tenant' and no 'subject' fields (local_facts.py:53). Both MemoryDataStore.find and PostgresDataStore.find match on row field equality/containment, so the filter matches zero rows. The granted local facts (whose key embeds subject for user-scoped grants) are never deleted, never listed under erased[], and never declared under retained[] — exactly the silent-hide the erasure contract forbids.
issues.failure_scenario: A subject with user-scoped onboarding grants requests erasure via /internal/privacy/erase. The onboarding_grants rows are left in place, the ack omits them from both 'erased' and 'retained', and if there were also no forced rows the response reports already_absent=true — a false 'she was erased' while personal-data-linked rows remain.

issues.title: Unencoded tenant/subject/fact interpolated into internal requirement-check URL
issues.detail: check() builds the URL by raw string substitution: path.replace('{fact}',fact).replace('{tenant}',tenant).replace('{subject}',subject) then base+path, with no URL/percent encoding (requirement_source/http.py:39-41). subject is attacker-influenced on the admin tier (/admin/inspect takes subject as a caller-supplied query param), and generally comes from token claims. A value containing '/', '?', '#', or '..' rewrites the request path or appends query params to the owning service's internal endpoint (CWE-88/CWE-918-adjacent request-path injection).
issues.failure_scenario: An operator (or a crafted subject claim) with value like '../admin/verified?force=1' or 'x?override=true' is substituted directly into the verification-service internal URL, redirecting the requirement check to a different internal path/query than intended and potentially returning a satisfied answer for a requirement that is not actually met.

issues.title: Keyset pagination cursor uses value['id'] but ORDER BY tie-breaks on row key
issues.detail: find() orders and compares by (COALESCE(value->>field,''), key) — the row's primary-key column — but encodes the next cursor from last.get('id') taken from the JSON value (postgres.py:200; MemoryDataStore has the same shape at memory.py:70). When a row's stored 'id' field is not identical to its storage key, the cursor's tie-break value no longer matches the ORDER BY tie-break column, so the tuple comparison on the next page can skip or duplicate rows sharing a sort-field value.
issues.failure_scenario: A collection is paginated where key != value['id'] and several rows share the same sort field (e.g. same 'created'); the second page's cursor comparison against `key` uses the mismatched id, dropping or repeating rows at the page boundary during a sweep or export.

issues.title: DSAR subject erasure is a silent no-op (wrong collection) — index keeps erased persons
issues.detail: SearchErasure.erase() queries the datastore collection _DOCS = "documents" (line 21) via store.find("documents", {"tenant":..,"owner":..}). But the actual index writes documents to a DIFFERENT collection: BuiltinIndex uses _DOCS = "search_docs" (adapters/index/builtin.py line 15, key "<index>:<doc_id>"). The "documents" collection is never written by this service, so find() always returns zero rows. The erase therefore deletes nothing, and even if the collection name matched it deletes only the raw doc row via store.delete and never scrubs the inverted-index postings (search_postings) or meta, so the person's terms remain fully searchable. Worse, the ack returns already_absent=True / erased=[] falsely reporting a successful erasure to compliance-service.
issues.failure_scenario: compliance-service fans out a DSAR erase for tenant T subject S whose name was indexed. POST /internal/privacy/erase returns {"erased":[],"already_absent":true} while a subsequent POST /api/v1/search for S's name still returns the document. GDPR/PDPL right-to-erasure is violated and the audit trail records a completed erasure that never happened.
issues.resolution: FIXED: erasure.py re-queries search_docs and deletes each doc via the index engine (postings+meta+row); returns erased:[search_docs:N].

issues.title: Cross-tenant document overwrite/hijack: storage key omits tenant
issues.detail: Documents are stored under _dk(index, doc_id) = f"{index}:{doc_id}" (lines 28-29) with tenant only a field inside the record, not part of the key; postings are keyed (index, term) too. On upsert, _remove_existing (lines 35-48) deletes any existing record with that (index, doc_id) regardless of its tenant, then writes the new record under the caller's tenant. The internal /search/index route (api/internal.py lines 99-108) lets any authenticated peer choose both index and tenant freely. Two tenants sharing an index name and a doc id collide: a peer indexing for tenant A can silently destroy or re-own tenant B's document. The read path filters by tenant so this is not a read leak, but it is cross-tenant data loss / record hijacking on the write path.
issues.failure_scenario: Tenant B has doc index="contacts", id="c-100". A peer indexing for tenant A calls POST /internal/search/index with index="contacts", id="c-100", tenant="A". _remove_existing wipes B's postings/meta and the record is rewritten with tenant=A; B's document is gone (and B's document count in meta is corrupted).
issues.resolution: FIXED: builtin upsert raises CrossTenantConflict when an existing (index,doc_id) belongs to another tenant; _remove_existing is tenant-guarded.

issues.title: Internal delete ignores tenant — cross-tenant document deletion
issues.detail: SearchService.delete(index, doc_id, tenant) (lines 71-74) calls self._index.delete(index=index, doc_id=doc_id) with NO tenant, and BuiltinIndex.delete -> _remove_existing (builtin.py lines 65-66, 35-48) removes by (index, doc_id) only. The DeleteIn body (api/internal.py lines 40-43, 120-128) requires a tenant but it is never used to verify the target record actually belongs to that tenant. Any internal peer can delete another tenant's document by supplying the right index+id (entity ids are often predictable), causing cross-tenant data loss.
issues.failure_scenario: A peer acting for tenant A calls POST /internal/search/delete {index:"orders", id:"o-42", tenant:"A"} where o-42 actually belongs to tenant B. The tenant field is ignored and B's document is deleted.
issues.resolution: FIXED: internal delete + core delete + port now thread tenant; _remove_existing returns early on tenant mismatch.

issues.title: Rate limiting fully built but wired to zero routes
issues.detail: build_policy/register_ratelimit_refund and the rate_limit dependency are constructed in main.py (lines 122-124) and defined here, but grep shows no route anywhere adds Depends(rate_limit) — not the user search/suggest routes (api/v1/search.py) nor the internal routes (api/internal.py). No middleware enforces it either. The entire limiter (including the RateLimit-* headers and fail-closed logic) is dead code, so every endpoint, including the expensive unbounded search path, is unthrottled. (The file header even still says "identity-service", a copy-paste indicator.)
issues.failure_scenario: An authenticated caller floods POST /api/v1/search with broad queries; nothing rate-limits them and the per-query cost (see the unbounded-candidate finding) amplifies into a service-wide DoS.
issues.resolution: FIXED: search POST + suggest GET now Depends(rate_limit); catalogue/stats also rate-limited.

issues.title: Unbounded candidate materialization on the search hot path (DoS)
issues.detail: _run builds candidate_tf as the full union of every term's posting list (lines 119-125), then loops over ALL candidates doing one datastore get per candidate (line 131), ranks all of them, and only paginates AFTER (lines 142-146). The only cost limits are query length and term count (core/query.py); there is no cap on posting-list size or candidate count. A single common term matching millions of docs triggers millions of per-doc datastore reads and full in-memory ranking per request. Because postings are shared across tenants in an index, a query also fetches other tenants' matching docs (filtered out at line 132) — pure read amplification. Combined with the missing rate limiter this is an easy DoS.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant on a large shared index searches a single high-frequency term; the request reads and ranks the entire posting union (all tenants' matching docs) before returning one page, spiking latency/memory and blocking the single-worker event loop.
issues.resolution: FIXED: _run caps candidate_tf at SEARCH_MAX_CANDIDATES (config, default 10_000) and breaks.

issues.title: suggest() scans up to 1,000,000 rows of the whole corpus on a user hot path
issues.detail: iter_docs (lines 77-79) calls self._store.list(_DOCS, _SCAN) with _SCAN = 1_000_000 (line 18), i.e. scan_all across ALL indexes and ALL tenants, pulling up to a million records into memory, THEN filters by index and slices [:limit]. This runs on the user-facing GET /api/v1/search/suggest and internal /search/suggest for every keystroke-style autocomplete call. The 'bounded by list_limit' claim in SearchService.suggest is false at the store layer — list_limit is applied only after the million-row read. On postgres this is a LIMIT 1000000 heap read per call.
issues.failure_scenario: Autocomplete on a service with a large search_docs collection: each /search/suggest request loads up to 1M rows into the process, causing memory pressure and multi-second latency; a few concurrent typers exhaust the worker.
issues.resolution: FIXED: suggest scan bounded to _SUGGEST_SCAN=10_000 (was 1_000_000).

issues.title: Index stats/catalogue leak global cross-tenant counts despite documented tenant re-scoping
issues.detail: GET /api/v1/search/indexes and GET /api/v1/search/indexes/{index}/stats are gated by _ADMIN = platform.search OR search.manage. search.manage is documented as a tenant-scoped operator capability (user_actions.py: 're-scopes to the caller's tenant on every call'), but the code does no tenant scoping: SearchService.stats/list_indexes (search_service.py lines 212-217) and BuiltinIndex.stats/list_indexes (builtin.py lines 74-88) return the global meta rows — index names across all tenants and aggregate n_docs/total_len that count every tenant's documents in a shared index. A tenant operator thus learns other tenants' index names and document volumes, and the documented isolation invariant is violated.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant admin holding search.manage calls GET /api/v1/search/indexes and sees every index name in the platform plus global document counts, and /indexes/{index}/stats returns n_docs including other tenants' docs.
issues.resolution: FIXED: /indexes and /stats now platform.search only (require_any_capability(platform.search)); tenant operator (search.manage) gets 403.

issues.title: Reported total shrinks across pages (computed after cursor filtering)
issues.detail: In _run, when a cursor is supplied, ordered is filtered to only hits AFTER the cursor position (lines 143-144) and THEN total = len(ordered) (line 145). So 'total' is the number of REMAINING results, not the total match count. Each subsequent page reports a smaller total, breaking clients that render 'N results' or compute page counts from total; next_cursor's guard (total > size, line 156) is also evaluated against the shrunken value.
issues.failure_scenario: A query with 100 matches and size=20: page 1 reports total=100, page 2 reports total=80, page 3 total=60, etc., so any UI or caller using total for pagination math is wrong on every page after the first.
issues.resolution: FIXED: total computed before cursor filtering; next_cursor emitted only when more results remain.

issues.title: SSRF DNS-rebinding: validated/pinned IP is discarded; ffmpeg connects by hostname
issues.detail: validate_source_url() (app/core/ssrf.py:66) resolves the host, blocks metadata/private/loopback IPs, and RETURNS a Resolved(ip=...) so the caller can pin the connection — the module docstring explicitly promises 'the caller can PIN the connection to it (DNS-rebinding safe)'. But StreamService._check_ssrf (line 354) throws the return value away, and start_session/probe_source pass the original hostname URL (spec.source_url = url) to the engine. FfmpegStreamEngine._input_args/probe (app/adapters/stream/ffmpeg_engine.py:38,140) invoke ffmpeg/ffprobe with '-i <hostname-url>', so ffmpeg does its OWN DNS resolution at connect time. The validation and the connection resolve the name independently.
issues.failure_scenario: Attacker (tenant operator) registers a source at http://evil.example/. evil.example resolves to a public IP during register_source and start_session validation (passes), then flips its DNS A record to 169.254.169.254 (or 10.x internal). When ffmpeg opens the URL milliseconds later it re-resolves to the internal/metadata IP and the stream engine proxies cloud-metadata / internal services. The whole point of the SSRF guard (re-validate at connect time, rebinding-safe) is defeated because the connection is never pinned to the validated IP.

issues.title: onvif.host is never SSRF-validated; PTZ connects to an arbitrary host
issues.detail: register_source SSRF-validates only `url` (self._check_ssrf(url)); the caller-supplied `onvif` dict (SourceIn.onvif in app/api/v1/stream.py:63) is stored verbatim (models.py:45). PTZ routes call _ptz_source() which returns src.onvif, and OnvifPtzController._default_factory (app/adapters/stream/onvif_ptz.py:22) does ONVIFCamera(onvif.get('host'), int(onvif.get('port',80)), ...) — an HTTP client to that host:port. No validate_source_url is ever applied to onvif.host, so the SSRF guard that protects `url` is fully bypassed via the onvif field.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant with stream.manage registers a source with onvif={'host':'169.254.169.254','port':80} and calls POST /sources/{id}/ptz/move or /ptz/presets. The service issues HTTP requests to the cloud-metadata endpoint (or any internal host/port), turning an authenticated operator action into an internal-network / metadata SSRF — exactly what the SSRF module exists to prevent for operator-supplied source targets.

issues.title: Global concurrency cap (STREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS_GLOBAL) is advertised but never enforced
issues.detail: StreamConfig stores max_concurrent_global (line 63) from STREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS_GLOBAL (config.py:469, wired in app/api/v1/stream.py:39), but _enforce_quota (line 349-352) only checks max_concurrent_per_tenant via count_live_for_tenant. There is no count_live_global / global check anywhere (grep confirms max_concurrent_global has no reader). The knob is a no-op.
issues.failure_scenario: Operator sets STREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS_GLOBAL=100 expecting a fleet-wide ceiling. With N tenants each allowed their per-tenant cap, total live sessions (each an ffmpeg process) grows without bound past the intended global limit, exhausting node CPU/memory/FDs — a resource-exhaustion DoS the operator believes is capped but is not.

issues.title: Concurrency quota is check-then-create (TOCTOU); cap can be exceeded under concurrent starts
issues.detail: start_session calls await self._enforce_quota(tenant) (line 121), which does count_live_for_tenant(...) >= cap, and only later awaits self._sessions.create(sess) (line 149). The count and the create are separate awaits with no atomic reservation/CAS. The same non-atomic gap exists for one_session_per_source (line 122-125: list_for_tenant then create).
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant at cap-1 live sessions fires K concurrent POST /sessions requests. Each coroutine reads count = cap-1 (< cap) before any create commits, all pass the guard, and all create sessions — leaving cap-1+K live sessions, over the per-tenant limit (and, with one_session_per_source, two live sessions on the same camera). Quota/billing/resource limits are silently breached.

issues.title: RecordingShipper has no lease/lock: concurrent sweeps double-ship segments and lose appends
issues.detail: ship_session lists rec_* files, then for each: reads bytes, put_segment to the sink, appends {ref,...} to rec.segments and rec.total_bytes, os.remove(local), and finally recordings.save(rec) (lines 34-72). Dedup relies solely on os.remove having deleted the local file. The /internal/stream/sweep endpoint (api/internal.py:76) calls ship_live_recordings with no locking, and it is CronJob/multi-replica driven. Two concurrent runs list the same not-yet-removed segments, both put_segment + append, and the two RecordingStore.save() calls are last-write-wins (get→append→put, no CAS in stores.py:104).
issues.failure_scenario: Two sweep replicas (or an overlapping cron) run concurrently: the same segment is uploaded twice and appended twice (duplicate segments / inflated total_bytes), OR the two get→append→save races drop one run's appended segments entirely (lost recording data). Also, if os.remove fails (OSError is swallowed, line 67-68) the segment re-ships on the next run regardless.

issues.title: Retention sweep scans the entire non-locked recordings table every run
issues.detail: iter_expired queries find(_RECORDINGS, {'locked': False}, sort=('started','asc')) and filters started < cutoff in Python (line 124-126). enforce_retention (stream_service.py:221-233) pages until cursor is exhausted. Because expired rows sort to the FRONT (asc), once a page crosses the cutoff every remaining row is non-expired, yet the loop keeps paging through all non-locked recordings — there is no early break when r['started'] >= cutoff.
issues.failure_scenario: With a large recordings table, each retention run reads the full non-locked collection page by page even though only the oldest few are expired, wasting datastore reads/latency that grows unbounded with retained history.

issues.title: Export range limit bypassable with non-ISO start/end timestamps
issues.detail: request() checks `end <= start` as a lexicographic string compare, then span = _span_seconds(start,end) and rejects span > max_range_seconds. _span_seconds (line 209-217) returns 0.0 on any parse failure. So non-ISO strings where end > start lexically (e.g. start='a', end='z') pass end<=start, yield span=0.0, and skip the EXPORT_MAX_RANGE_SECONDS check entirely; the row is created and enqueued.
issues.failure_scenario: A caller submits malformed start/end that pass the string ordering check; the range cap is silently not applied. Impact is limited (worker segment matching also uses string compare and finds no footage, producing an empty/failed export), but the documented safety limit is not enforced and unvalidated ranges reach the worker.

issues.title: close_sweep reads only the first `limit` tenants, so scheduled tenant erasures beyond that window are NEVER performed
issues.detail: close_sweep() calls self._repo.list(limit) which is store.scan_all('tenants', limit) — a bounded read of the FIRST `limit` rows in a deterministic order (postgres: ORDER BY key; memory: insertion order), NOT a query for tenants that are actually closing. It then filters that fixed prefix for status==SUSPENDED with an elapsed grace_until. The internal route POST /internal/tenants/close-sweep (app/api/internal.py:148-154) invokes it with the default limit=200 and no cursor/pagination. The docstring claims a deployment with more closing tenants than `limit` 'simply finishes them on the next pass', but every pass re-reads the SAME first `limit` rows, so a closing tenant whose key sorts after position `limit` is read on no pass and is never erased. Owner self-close (svc.close) promises erasure after the grace window; this silently breaks that guarantee and leaves suspended tenants' data retained indefinitely — a GDPR/data-retention failure that no test or metric surfaces.
issues.failure_scenario: Platform has 500 active tenants (keys sorted). Tenant whose key sorts at position 300 self-closes; grace elapses. Every scheduled close-sweep reads tenants at key-positions 1-200 only, never sees the closed tenant, returns erased=0 for it forever. Its data is retained permanently despite the completed close request.

issues.title: Slug/domain uniqueness is check-then-put with an await gap (TOCTOU), so concurrent provisions of the same slug/domain both succeed
issues.detail: create() does `if await store.get(_SLUGS, slug) is not None: raise SlugTaken` and then, after several awaits, `store.put(_SLUGS, slug, {id})`. There is no atomic put-if-absent / CAS. Between the get and the put the event loop yields, so two concurrent provision calls (POST /api/v1/tenants or POST /internal/tenants) for the same slug can both observe the slug as free, both write distinct tenant rows under new ids, and both write the slug index — the second overwrites the first. Result: two tenant rows exist for one slug, the slug index resolves to only one, and the other tenant row is orphaned (unreachable by slug/domain). The same race applies to the domain index (domain hijack: two tenants both claim a custom host). The comment in api/internal.py claims 'slug uniqueness IS the idempotency', but this non-atomic check cannot enforce it under concurrency.
issues.failure_scenario: Onboarding retries fire two concurrent POST /internal/tenants with slug='acme'. Both pass the get()==None check, both put tenant rows (id A, id B), both put tenant_slugs['acme']; B wins. Tenant A is now an orphaned, billable-but-unroutable registry row; the domain index can likewise be reassigned to a second tenant.

issues.title: Lifecycle audit is written ahead of the existence check, recording delete/suspend/reactivate events for tenants that were never mutated
issues.detail: delete() (line 160-171), suspend() (126-143) and reactivate() (146-157) call auditor.record(...) BEFORE _load(), which is the call that 404s on a missing/unknown tenant_id. When the tenant does not exist, the audit sink has already persisted a 'tenant.deleted' / 'tenant.suspended' / 'tenant.reactivated' entry attributing a destructive action that never happened to the operator, and the request then returns 404. Because these actions are critical and fail-closed, this also lets an attacker with platform.tenants generate audit-log noise / false attribution for arbitrary tenant_ids without any state change. The write-ahead rationale (do not 503 a caller whose mutation already succeeded) does not require recording before confirming the target even exists.
issues.failure_scenario: Operator (or a compromised platform token) calls DELETE /api/v1/tenants/does-not-exist. Audit log gains a 'tenant.deleted resource=tenant:does-not-exist actor=<operator>' entry; the endpoint returns 404 and nothing was deleted. The audit trail now shows deletions that never occurred.

issues.title: Self config/branding updates have no tenant-status guard; a suspended tenant keeps mutating, and a tombstoned tenant is partially rewritten
issues.detail: update_config() and set_branding() unconditionally merge into tenant.config/branding and call repo.update(), with no check on tenant.status. The self routes (PUT /api/v1/tenant/config and /branding) reach these for any principal holding tenant.manage whose token is still valid. A SUSPENDED tenant (including one suspended by owner-close within the grace window) can therefore keep editing its own config/branding despite being off the platform. Worse, if the token outlives a tombstone, _own -> _load returns the tombstone Tenant (status=deleted, config stripped to keep-fields) and update_config re-populates and re-persists config onto the deleted marker via repo.update(), writing attacker-controlled data back onto a record whose whole purpose is to be a minimal erasure marker.
issues.failure_scenario: Owner self-closes tenant (status=suspended, grace pending). With the still-valid session token they PUT /api/v1/tenant/config; the change is accepted and persisted even though access was supposed to have stopped, and the config write is not gated by the suspended state.

issues.title: Internal tenant view exposes the full config blob (including internal _close scheduling and closed_by actor) to any internal caller
issues.detail: _internal_view() returns fields listed in TENANT_INTERNAL_FIELDS, whose default (app/config.py:314) includes 'config'. tenant.config carries the service-internal '_close' object written by close() (app/core/tenant_service.py:168), which contains scheduled_at, grace_until and closed_by — the subject id of the operator/owner who closed the tenant. Any peer holding only the shared internal token (the default-open internal tier) reading GET /internal/tenants/{id} or /internal/tenants/resolve therefore receives internal lifecycle scheduling and an actor identifier that is not part of the tenant's public/business data. Least-privilege intent of the field allowlist is undercut because '_close' rides inside the broad 'config' field rather than being an explicitly chosen exposure.
issues.failure_scenario: A render/peer service calls GET /internal/tenants/{id} to fetch branding; the response also includes config._close.closed_by, leaking who closed the tenant and its erasure schedule to a service that had no need for it.

issues.title: DSAR erasure leaves raw PII (sender phone number) in ticket.ref
issues.detail: TicketErasure.erase() redacts a ticket's `subject` and clears `meta`, but never touches `ref`. Inbound-channel tickets are opened with ref={'kind': channel, 'id': sender} where `sender` is the customer's raw phone number (see inbound_bridge.py:95). The erase loop (lines 41-45) only sets row['subject']=[erased] and row['meta']={}, so after a DSAR the raw phone number persists in ref.id in the datastore. The service's own model docstring claims a ticket 'carries raiser_ref, not a person' and that erasure removes the mutable PII, but this identifier is left behind, defeating the erasure guarantee compliance-service relies on.
issues.failure_scenario: A WhatsApp message opens ticket T with ref={'kind':'whatsapp','id':'+9665...'}. Compliance runs POST /internal/privacy/erase for that subject. erase() redacts subject/meta and reports success, but ticket row T still contains ref.id='+9665...' (the raw phone) forever.

issues.title: Raw sender (phone number) persisted in plaintext as ticket ref and thread-index key
issues.detail: The module docstring states 'The sender (a phone number) is never stored raw', but _thread_key() (line 54) builds a persisted datastore key '{len}:{tenant}|{channel}|{sender}' embedding the raw sender, and ingest() writes ticket ref={'kind':channel,'id':sender} (line 95) with the raw sender. Both are written to the store in the clear (collections inbound_threads and tickets). Neither is pseudonymised, and neither is covered by TicketErasure (the thread index and ref are never redacted), so the raw phone number is stored at rest and is not erasable — contradicting the stated invariant and the pseudonymisation design used elsewhere.
issues.failure_scenario: Any inbound WhatsApp message causes '+96650...' to be stored verbatim as an inbound_threads row key and inside the ticket's ref.id, readable by anyone with datastore access and surviving a DSAR.

issues.title: Per-type reply_capability is parsed but never enforced
issues.detail: TicketType carries reply_capability (workflow.py:37, populated at workflow.py:152 from config, e.g. config.py:264/286), advertised as 'who may add a reply'. But TicketService.reply() (line 88) never checks it, and the route POST /tickets/{id}/replies (tickets.py:178) only requires _SELF (tickets.self OR tickets.manage OR platform.tickets) plus ownership. A ticket type that sets reply_capability to a stricter cap (e.g. 'tickets.manage', to make a type operator-reply-only) is silently ignored — any owning tickets.self holder can still reply. This is an advertised-but-unread authorization knob: the config accepts and stores it, but behaviour does not change, so an operator believes a restriction is in force that is not.
issues.failure_scenario: Admin configures a ticket type with reply_capability='tickets.manage' intending only staff may reply. A customer (tickets.self) who raised such a ticket POSTs a reply and it is accepted, because reply_capability is never consulted.

issues.title: Grantee scoped ticket list filters by scope AFTER a capped fetch, silently omitting covered tickets
issues.detail: list_shared_tickets() calls tickets.find(tenant=tenant, limit=cap+1) with NO scope filters pushed into the query, then filters in Python with grant.covers(r) (lines 316-320). find() returns only the newest cap+1 tickets by created-desc. If the tenant has more than cap+1 tickets and the grant is scoped (e.g. scope type=['billing']), covered tickets that are not among the newest cap+1 rows are never returned, and 'truncated' (len(covered) > cap) is computed from the pre-filter fetch so it under-reports. The grant's type/status scope is known and could be passed to TicketStore.find filters, but is not. There is also no cursor exposed, so a grantee cannot page to the omitted rows.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant has 5000 tickets; the newest 51 are all type='support'. A grantee with scope type=['billing'] calls GET /internal/tickets — covered=[] and truncated=false, so the grantee sees zero of the tenant's many billing tickets and is told nothing was hidden.

issues.title: Inbound idempotency claim is get-then-put (TOCTOU), not atomic compare-and-set
issues.detail: ingest() checks store.get(_INGESTED, ikey) is None (line 78) and then store.put()s the claim (line 82) as two separate operations with no atomic CAS. Two concurrent deliveries/re-polls of the same external_id can both observe None and both proceed to open/append a ticket, producing a duplicate. The docstring acknowledges the claim is 'BEFORE the ticket write' but the check-then-set is not atomic, so the dedupe guarantee only holds under the assumption of a single serial scheduler; any concurrency (two scheduler ticks, two pods) breaks it.
issues.failure_scenario: The drain/ingest endpoint is invoked twice concurrently (retry or overlapping schedule) with the same message batch; both calls see _INGESTED miss for wamid X and each open a ticket, so the customer's one message yields two tickets/replies.

issues.title: State transitions have no optimistic concurrency; concurrent moves last-write-wins
issues.detail: transition() fetches the ticket, checks can_transition on the current status, then sets t.status and save()s (lines 107-120) with a plain put (TicketStore.save -> datastore.put, no version/CAS). Two concurrent transitions from the same source status (e.g. new->resolved and new->rejected) can both pass the guard and both append status_changed events, leaving the projection with whichever wrote last while the event log records two contradictory terminal moves from the same state. assign()/tag() have the same last-write-wins behaviour on the projection.
issues.failure_scenario: Two operators simultaneously move ticket T from 'new'; both reads see status='new', both validate, both save. The log shows new->resolved AND new->rejected, and t.status is whichever put landed last — an inconsistent, unreproducible outcome.

issues.title: Empty/unconfigured verdict_ok makes an empty provider response read as VERIFIED (fail-open)
issues.detail: _read_verdict compares `value == self._p.get("verdict_ok", "").strip()`. When a provider profile has a verdict_path but no verdict_ok (default ""), and the provider's response contains an empty string at verdict_path, then value=="" and verdict_ok=="" match, returning Outcome(VERIFIED). This directly violates the file's own stated invariant ('Unrecognised never falls through to yes'). The production boot guard (config.py assert_verify_config_ok, line 435) requires verdict_path but never requires verdict_ok, so a service boots in production with this hole. Only a missing field (raw is None -> ERROR) is guarded; an empty-string field is not.
issues.failure_scenario: Operator configures VERIFY_PROFILES with provider.verdict_path=data.status but omits provider.verdict_ok. Provider returns HTTP 200 {"data":{"status":""}} (or any path resolving to "") for an unverified/failed claim -> service records verdict=verified and grants trust to an unverified identity.

issues.title: Async provider callback (resolve) is never wired to any route; PENDING verdicts can only expire, never succeed
issues.detail: VerificationService.resolve() is the documented idempotent callback that moves a PENDING async verification to VERIFIED/REFUSED. A repo-wide grep shows resolve() has no caller and no HTTP route in api/internal.py or api/v1/*. Providers configured with verdict_pending (the file's headline feature: 'Async is a real state', Nafath-style push) therefore produce PENDING records that only ever lapse to EXPIRED via sweep_pending. No async verification can ever succeed.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant configures a Nafath-style provider that returns AWAITING_USER (mapped to verdict_pending). The user approves on their phone, but there is no endpoint for the provider's callback to reach resolve(); the record sits PENDING until pending_until, then sweep_pending marks it EXPIRED. A legitimately verified user is never verified.

issues.title: ORDER BY index does not match the sort key used by every verification query
issues.detail: The shipped btree index kv_created_desc is on `(collection, COALESCE(value->>'created',''), key)`, but every VerificationStore query (stores.py latest/for_subject/pending_before/pending_reviews, lines 47,52,59,67) sorts by created_at, producing ORDER BY COALESCE(value->>'created_at','') in find(). The index field ('created') never matches the ORDER BY field ('created_at'), so Postgres cannot use it to order — exactly the mismatched-index bitmap-scan + top-N sort the adapter's own comment (lines 24-30) warns against. pending_reviews and pending_before scan and sort all matching rows on every request/sweep.
issues.failure_scenario: A tenant with a large verification history calls GET /verification/claims or the review queue: Postgres GIN-filters then sorts all of the tenant's (or all PENDING) rows in memory O(rows) instead of an O(page) index scan, degrading under load.

issues.title: IdentityRegistry.remember is a non-atomic get-then-put, weakening once-per-identity anti-abuse
issues.detail: remember() does `existing = await store.get(_SEEN, claim_ref)` then branches to put a new row (first_seen=True) or increment. There is no CAS/atomic upsert on the count, so two concurrent verifications of the same identity both read existing=None, both write a fresh row with first_seen=True/times=1, and one clobbers the other. This is the exact anti-abuse invariant the collection exists to protect (per the module docstring: stop a repeat welcome-gift by recognising the same registration).
issues.failure_scenario: Attacker fires two verify() requests for the same commercial registration simultaneously (different tenants). Both remember() calls observe no prior row and record first_seen; the 'seen before' count is 1 not 2, and downstream once-per-identity grant logic reading this signal can be induced to treat a repeat identity as first-seen.

issues.title: decide() has no optimistic concurrency; concurrent reviews can lose updates / double-settle
issues.detail: decide() reads the record, checks verdict not in (VERIFIED,REFUSED), then mutates and put()s with no version/CAS check. Two concurrent decisions on the same PENDING record both pass the settled-check and both write; under two-eyes, two concurrent first-approvals each read reviewers=[] and each write their own single-element reviewers list, overwriting the other, so the two-eyes accumulation is lost.
issues.failure_scenario: Two reviewers approve the same claim at the same time under VERIFY_TWO_EYES: each reads provider_state.reviewers=[], each writes reviewers=[self]; the last write wins with one reviewer recorded, neither the completion nor a correct two-eyes tally results.

issues.title: Idempotency row loses its version on finalize; Postgres re-claim after TTL is permanently stuck at 409
issues.detail: _claim() atomically claims a slot with store.cas(..., expected_version=0/N, ...) which stamps a version. But _finalize() (line 266) writes the finished result with a plain store.put({'result':..., 'expires_at':...}) that carries NO version field. On the Postgres datastore, put() upserts the value verbatim, so the finished idempotency row ends up with no 'version' key. When the result TTL later expires and the SAME source is presented again, _claim() falls through to the re-claim branch: expected = int(row.get('version',0)) = 0, then store.cas(key, 0, ...). PostgresDataStore.cas() treats expected==0 as INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (postgres.py:248-254), which returns 0 rows because the key already exists -> won=False -> (False, None) -> caller raises Conflict('WALLET_OP_IN_PROGRESS'). The slot can never be re-claimed and never replays. On the in-memory store the same path works (cas with expected 0 matches a versionless row), so this is also a silent memory-vs-postgres behavioural divergence that tests on memory will not catch.
issues.failure_scenario: credit(source='psp_settlement_123') runs and finalizes on Postgres. >24h later (WALLET_IDEMPOTENCY_TTL_SECONDS elapsed) the PSP redelivers settlement 'psp_settlement_123'. Instead of a clean replay or re-execution, credit() returns HTTP 409 forever and never resolves.
issues.resolution: FIXED: _finalize carries the row version forward so a post-TTL re-claim stays on the Postgres cas UPDATE branch (was permanently stuck at 409; also a memory/postgres divergence). Regression: test_audit_fixes.py.

issues.title: sweep_grants claws back money attributed to a different grant on the same fund (mixed policies)
issues.detail: sweep_grants computes spare = int(w.funds.get(grant.fund,0)) - int(w.held.get(grant.fund,0)) (line 719) and claws remaining = max(0, min(spare, grant.amount)). This is a FUND-GLOBAL figure; the service never tracks per-grant consumption. When two grants share one fund but carry DIFFERENT frozen policies and the customer has spent part of the pool, an expiring 'forfeit' grant will forfeit balance that logically belongs to a still-active 'extend'/'dormant' grant, because it assumes its own remainder is still whole. Money the platform intended to preserve (dormant/extend) is irreversibly clawed back (clawback). With a single policy per fund the accounting is fungible and harmless; the defect appears only with mixed policies on one fund.
issues.failure_scenario: Fund 'promo' has grant A (100, forfeit, expires today) and grant B (100, extend, expires next month); customer spent 100 from the fungible 200. Balance=100, held=0. sweep_grants on A: spare=100, remaining=min(100,100)=100 -> clawback 100, leaving 0. B's 100 that should have been auto-extended is gone.
issues.resolution: VERIFIED REAL. Requires a money-accounting decision (how pooled spend attributes across grants with mixed idle policies on one fund). The service tracks no per-grant consumption. Surfaced to Tamam before choosing a model (conservative under-claw vs FIFO per-grant tracking). Not silently fixed.

issues.title: reconcile() is an unbounded O(seq) sequential read on request-exposed endpoints
issues.detail: reconcile() loops `for seq in range(1, w.seq + 1)` issuing one store.get(_LEDGER, key) per ledger entry (line 216-217). It is exposed at GET /internal/wallet/{tenant}/reconcile (internal.py:148) and GET /api/v1/wallet/admin/reconcile (wallet.py:110). Unlike ledger() (clamped to LEDGER_LIST_LIMIT) and the sweepers (paged), reconcile has no bound: a tenant with a large ledger forces millions of sequential round-trips inside a single HTTP request. On Postgres each get() is a separate pool acquire + query, so this both starves the connection pool and can run for minutes, a denial-of-service vector reachable by any platform operator or internal caller.
issues.failure_scenario: A high-volume tenant accumulates ~2M ledger entries. A single call to /api/v1/wallet/admin/reconcile?tenant=X issues ~2M sequential SELECTs, holding a pool slot and blocking for minutes; a few concurrent calls exhaust DATASTORE_POOL_MAX and stall the service.
issues.resolution: FIXED: reconcile() bounded by RECONCILE_MAX_ENTRIES (config, default 20000); past the cap it returns consistent=None/LEDGER_TOO_LARGE instead of an unbounded sequential request-path scan. Regression: test_audit_fixes.py.

issues.title: withdraw() double-pays on retry when source is empty despite documented idempotency
issues.detail: withdraw()'s docstring states 'Idempotent by source, so a retried request never pays out twice', but _claim() returns (True, None) immediately when source is falsy (line 240-241 opt-out). The internal route defines source with default '' (internal.py:88), so a caller (or a network-level retry) that omits source gets NO idempotency: each call writes a new PENDING Withdrawal and debits withdrawable funds again. Because this is money LEAVING the platform, a silent idempotency opt-out on empty source is a double-payout footgun that contradicts the stated guarantee (refund() deliberately avoids this by keying on the spend seq instead of the caller source).
issues.failure_scenario: A payout orchestrator POSTs /internal/wallet/withdraw {tenant, amount:50000} with no source, the response is lost to a timeout, and it retries. Two PENDING withdrawals are created and the balance is debited 100000; two external transfers execute.
issues.resolution: FIXED: withdraw() now requires a non-empty source (WITHDRAW_SOURCE_REQUIRED) - money leaving must be idempotent; empty-source opt-out is refused. Regression: test_audit_fixes.py.

issues.title: confirm/release audit rows record an empty tenant
issues.detail: The confirm and release routes record audit with tenant=str(result.get('tenant','')) (internal.py:250 and 264), but WalletService.confirm()/release() results never include a 'tenant' key (confirm returns {'hold_id','state','released', **out} where out is {'funds','held','balance','entry'}). So every wallet.confirmed / wallet.released audit row is written with tenant='' , weakening cross-tenant attribution of money-consuming actions in the audit trail (the hold_id resource is still present, but the tenant dimension a review filters on is blank).
issues.failure_scenario: During an incident review, filtering audit records by tenant misses all confirm/release events for the affected tenant because they were all recorded with an empty tenant field.
issues.resolution: FIXED: confirm()/release() results include tenant on every return path, so wallet.confirmed/released audit rows are attributable. Regression: test_audit_fixes.py.

issues.title: Critical wallet.credited audit written before input validation, logging credits that never happened
issues.detail: The credit route records the critical wallet.credited audit row (write-ahead) at internal.py:160 BEFORE calling WalletService.credit(), which then validates the fund and raises WalletError('UNKNOWN_FUND:...') at wallet_service.py:276-277 (and require_non_negative before that). A request naming a non-existent fund (or otherwise rejected before any mutation) still emits a critical money-creation audit event, producing a false 'credit' record for an action that moved no money. This pollutes exactly the insider-fraud trail that marking wallet.credited critical is meant to keep trustworthy.
issues.failure_scenario: POST /internal/wallet/credit {tenant, fund:'nonexistent', amount:1000} is rejected with 400 UNKNOWN_FUND, yet a wallet.credited audit row for tenant/1000 is already in the tamper-evident chain, implying a credit that never occurred.
issues.resolution: FIXED: validate_credit() runs in the credit route BEFORE the write-ahead wallet.credited audit, so a rejected credit no longer emits a critical money-creation row. Regression: test_audit_fixes.py.

issues.title: Circuit-open / disabled deliveries are never re-scheduled, so they permanently occupy the sweep budget (head-of-line starvation)
issues.detail: On the early-return paths in deliver() — circuit_open (lines 162-163) and endpoint_disabled (lines 156-157) — the delivery's status stays QUEUED/FAILED and next_retry_at is left unchanged (still <= now). DeliveryStore.due() (stores.py:170-187) selects exactly the rows with status in {queued,failed} and next_retry_at <= now, sorted by created ASC, up to list_limit (default 100). So these deliveries remain 'due' on every single sweep tick forever. deliver() re-processes them and returns immediately without progress, and because they are the oldest they crowd out deliverable rows for healthy endpoints.
issues.failure_scenario: One customer disables an endpoint (or an endpoint's circuit opens) that has >100 QUEUED deliveries. Every /internal/webhooks/sweep tick, due() fills its entire 100-row budget with those perpetually-due, oldest-first rows; deliver() returns 'endpoint_disabled'/'circuit_open' for each and advances nothing. Deliverable webhooks for every other tenant behind them never get sent — a single dead endpoint stalls fleet-wide delivery (availability DoS) and the sweeper busy-loops on the same rows.

issues.title: httpx transport IP-pinning is defeated for IPv6-resolved hosts, reopening the SSRF/DNS-rebinding window (and breaking IPv6 delivery)
issues.detail: The pin is applied by string surgery: pinned = url.replace(f'//{host}', f'//{pinned_ip}', 1). host comes from urlsplit(url).hostname, which returns IPv6 addresses UNBRACKETED, whereas the URL authority contains them BRACKETED ('//[2001:db8::1]'). The replace therefore never matches, so pinned == the original URL and httpx connects by RE-RESOLVING the hostname itself — exactly the TOCTOU/rebinding window core.ssrf.validate() pinned an IP to close. Even for an ordinary hostname whose validated address is IPv6, the substituted authority '//2001:db8::1/...' is malformed, so the connection either misparses or fails. Contrast StdlibTransport (the default), which connects to the pinned_ip directly with correct AF_INET6 handling.
issues.failure_scenario: With WEBHOOK_TRANSPORT_DRIVER=httpx, an attacker registers an endpoint on a hostname that resolves to a public IPv6 at validation time, then flips DNS to an internal IPv6 (or link-local) before the delivery attempt. Because the pin is silently not applied, httpx re-resolves and connects to the attacker-controlled internal target — SSRF against internal services. Separately, legitimate IPv6-only endpoints can never receive deliveries.

issues.title: deliver() has no compare-and-set on the DELIVERING transition, allowing concurrent double-send of the same delivery
issues.detail: deliver() guards only against DELIVERED/DEAD (line 149), then sets d.status=DELIVERING and saves (lines 171-173) with no atomic CAS from the prior status. Two concurrent invocations — e.g. the sweep loop and a manual POST /internal/webhooks/deliver/{id}, or two overlapping sweeps — both read the same QUEUED/FAILED row, both pass the guard, and both perform the outbound HTTP send.
issues.failure_scenario: A sweep tick picks delivery dlv_X (QUEUED) at the same moment an operator calls the internal deliver route for dlv_X. Both send the webhook to the customer endpoint, producing a duplicate delivery. Only the consumer's Idempotency-Key dedupe prevents a duplicate downstream side effect; the service itself provides no once-only guarantee at the transition.

issues.title: Inbound dedupe (seen -> record) is not atomic, so concurrent duplicate events are published twice
issues.detail: ingest() checks store.seen() (line 54) and only later calls store.record() (line 59) and _publish() (line 60). There is no atomic reserve/insert-if-absent. Two concurrent requests carrying the same (source, provider_event_id) both observe seen()==False, both record (second overwrites the first by key) and both publish to the event bus.
issues.failure_scenario: A provider (or an attacker replaying within the signature tolerance window) sends the same signed event twice near-simultaneously. Both pass the dedupe check and both fire inbound.<source> onto the EventBus, so downstream subscribers process the same third-party event twice despite the documented once-only intent.

issues.title: 3xx responses are classified as retryable and retried to exhaustion instead of treated as terminal
issues.detail: classify() (lines 31-41) returns 'delivered' only for 2xx, 'terminal' for 4xx (except 408/429), and falls through to 'retryable' for everything else — which includes 3xx. The transports do not follow redirects (httpx Client defaults follow_redirects=False; the stdlib transport issues a single request). So a customer endpoint answering 301/302/307 is retried up to RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS (8) with backoff and then dead-lettered, though it will never succeed.
issues.failure_scenario: A customer moves their endpoint and returns 301 to the new URL. Every delivery to that endpoint burns all 8 retries over the full backoff window and lands in the DLQ, wasting worker capacity and delaying the dead-letter signal, when the response is deterministically non-retryable.

issues.title: PIH captured at slot-allocation time forks the ICV/PIH chain under deferred or out-of-order signing
issues.detail: allocate_slot() freezes an invoice's PIH from head.last_hash (the last SIGNED invoice's hash) at the moment the slot is reserved, and build_ubl() then bakes that PIH into the unsigned draft XML (zatca_service.finalize lines 51-60, ubl.py line 113). But signing is explicitly deferred/retryable on a signer outage or not-onboarded tenant (zatca_service._defer, _sign), and finalize has no per-tenant ordering lock, so invoice N can be allocated before invoice N-1 is signed. record_hash only advances head.last_hash for the highest-ICV signed invoice, so N's PIH ends up pointing at an older invoice's hash, not N-1's actual hash. chain.verify_chain() enforces pih == prev.hash (line 28) and ZATCA reporting/clearance enforces the same, so the invoice is rejected and the taxpayer's chain is permanently broken from that ICV onward.
issues.failure_scenario: Signer is briefly unavailable. finalize(number=5) allocates ICV 5 with PIH=hash(4) but sign fails -> stays pending. finalize(number=6) allocates ICV 6, head.last_hash is still hash(4) (5 never signed), so PIH(6)=hash(4). Signer recovers; 5 and 6 both sign. Invoice 6's PIH is hash(4), not hash(5). verify_chain returns pih_mismatch at ICV 6 and ZATCA rejects invoice 6 and every later invoice.

issues.title: build_zatca() never receives the invoice's tenant, so per-tenant signer credentials are silently ignored
issues.detail: build_zatca(request, tenant="") resolves the signer credential via `await creds.token(tenant)` (lines 37-40), but every caller invokes build_zatca(request) with no tenant: the internal finalize (internal.py line 76), internal/admin sweep, onboard_compliance/onboard_production, and all admin invoice routes. SignerCredentials.token("") (operator_credentials.py line 34) therefore only ever reads the platform-wide (tenant "") stored/config token. The entire per-tenant operator-credential feature (set_secret with a tenant, _invalidate(tenant)) is dead for signing and onboarding: a per-tenant ZATCA_SIGNER_TOKEN set through the operator panel is written and cached under tenant X but never consulted when finalizing or onboarding tenant X.
issues.failure_scenario: Operator sets a tenant-specific signer token for tenant X via PUT /operator/secrets {tenant: X}. finalize for an invoice of tenant X calls build_zatca(request) (tenant ""), which resolves token("") = the platform token, signing tenant X's invoices with the wrong sidecar credential (or failing) while the panel reports the tenant credential as set.

issues.title: Retry sweep reads the entire pending backlog every run when few invoices are due
issues.detail: due_for_retry() pushes the three unfinished statuses into the datastore but filters next_retry_at in Python (lines 111-114), looping `while len(out) < limit` and paging _PAGE=500 rows at a time until the cursor is exhausted. When only a handful of invoices are actually due, `out` never reaches `limit`, so the loop reads EVERY pending/signed/submitted invoice across all tenants on every sweep. sweep() runs on a schedule (POST /sweep and /internal/zatca/sweep), so with a large steady-state backlog of not-yet-due invoices each sweep is O(total unfinished invoices) instead of O(due).
issues.failure_scenario: 100,000 invoices sit in 'pending' with next_retry_at in the future (e.g. capped or long-backoff). A sweep needing to process 3 due invoices still fetches all 100,000 rows in 200 datastore pages before returning, on every scheduled sweep tick.

issues.title: Internal finalize promises 'never fails the caller' but raises 500 on a malformed line or currency
issues.detail: The finalize route validates only that invoice.number is present (line 74); build_ubl() then does `int(ln["amount_minor"])` for each line (ubl.py line 55) and raises ValueError on a non-3-letter currency (line 48). finalize() (zatca_service.py) does not wrap build_ubl in try/except, so a line missing amount_minor (KeyError), a non-integer amount, or a bad currency propagates out as an unhandled 500 — contradicting the documented guarantee that finalize never fails the caller and leaves nothing retryable.
issues.failure_scenario: A caller posts /internal/zatca/finalize with invoice.lines=[{"description":"x"}] (no amount_minor). build_ubl raises KeyError('amount_minor'), which is not caught, returning HTTP 500 instead of a 422 or a retryable pending invoice.
